title: The Glass Garden
story:
In the quiet of the Botanical Mezzanine, the giant parchment pages turned with the soft sound of dry leaves rustling underfoot. James leaned over the cedar drafting table, holding Barnaby's brass magnifying lens steady over a hand-tinted folio of highland flora. Through the curved glass, every veined leaf became a river delta. Through the curved glass, every dried spore became a miniature world. Through the curved glass, every faded ink inscription became a trail of black ants marching across the page. He had lived his entire life beneath leaves just like these in the Great Canopy, but he had never paused to see the tiny architecture holding them together.

As he carefully lifted a brittle vellum sheet detailing specimens gathered along the high ridges near the Whispering Flats, something fell out with a light, dry click. It was small, woody, and shaped like a five-pointed star no larger than an acorn cap, untouched by rot or dust. James held it close to his nose. It smelled faintly of sun-warmed cedar and clean mountain air—not like the coal-smoke and oily puddles of Oakhaven, but like the open ridge where he had first stepped into the wider world. He unstoppered his brass canister and slipped the star-pod inside beside Barnaby's map, feeling the quiet satisfaction of tucking away a secret.

At the far end of the gallery, a pair of tall arched glass doors stood slightly ajar, letting in a warm, damp draft that smelled entirely different from old paper. Drawn by the earthy scent, James padded across the floorboards and nudged the iron latch with his shoulder. He stepped across the threshold and into the Grand Library's Solarium—a soaring glass greenhouse perched high against the library's sunlit southern flank, alive with climbing vines, dwarf citrus trees, and the faint, sleepy hum of indoor bees.

Here, the golden morning light poured unrestricted through diamond-paned glass ribs, framing the slate rooftops and smoking chimneys of Oakhaven far below. James stood on the warm terracotta tiles, his leather strap resting comfortably against his chest, watching a pale yellow moth flutter between white lemon blossoms. He wondered how many secret forests humans had hidden away inside their mountains of stone.
